title: Best Estimating Software for General Contractors in 2026: 10 Tools Compared
summary: Compare the best healthcare construction and fit-out software. Manage hospital renovations, compliance, budgets, procurement, and phasing.

## **Key Takeaways**


- The best estimating software for general contractors depends on where you lose margin: RDash for post-award cost control, STACK or Togal.AI for takeoff.


- Already on Procore, Autodesk Forma, or Sage? Start with that vendor’s estimating module, because the estimate flows into budgets without a new integration.


- Small builders and remodelers get the most for their money from Buildxact, Contractor Foreman or Clear Estimates; check each plan’s user limit.


- US nonresidential input prices rose 7.1% in the year to June 2026, about double contractors’ 3.5% bid-price rise, so outdated rates erode margin.


- Where vendors publish prices, plans run from free to $349 per user per month; Procore, Sage and ProEst quote privately.


- AI takeoff saves hours, but Duane Morris attorneys expect contractors to be held responsible for AI quantity errors, like any estimator’s mistake.


- Before buying, trace one line item from drawing to purchase order; three or more retypes means handoffs, not takeoff, are your problem.


**The best estimating software for a general contractor is the one that keeps your bid intact after you win it.** Takeoff speed matters, but margin is rarely lost because a measurement took an extra hour. It leaks in the handoffs between the bid, the purchase orders, and the cost report.


This guide compares 10 tools on both halves of that job: how quickly each one gets you to a priced bid, and how far that bid travels into purchasing and cost control after award.

## **How We Chose and Ranked These 10 Tools**


**We ranked each tool on how far it carries a number from the drawing or BOQ to the job’s final cost report, using only what each vendor publishes on its own website as of October 2026.**


We scored every tool on five things:


1. **Coverage of the estimate chain:** Does it quantify, price, compete, commit, and control, or only some of those?


2. **Evidence:** Every feature and price below comes from the vendor’s own product or pricing page. Where a vendor does not publish a price, we say so instead of repeating third-party guesses.


3. **Fit by how work arrives:** Measuring from drawings on hard-bid work is a different job from pricing a client-issued bill of quantities.


4. **Cost at real team sizes,** not just the headline “from” price.


5. **Honest limits:** Each review ends with what the tool is not built for.


**Why there are no star ratings:** Review counts across these products range from a few dozen to several thousand, and some directory listings blend a whole platform into one score. A 4.5 for one tool and a 4.5 for another rarely measure the same thing, so we left them out.


## **Why the Best Estimate Is the One That Survives the Job**


**Construction margins are thin enough that an accurate estimate still loses money if its quantities and rates get retyped, repriced, or dropped between the bid and the purchase order.**


The numbers leave little slack. In


[Aswath Damodaran’s January 2026 dataset](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/margin.html) , 48 US-listed engineering and construction companies averaged a net margin of 5.94%, and those are the large, listed firms.


KPMG’s


[2023 Global Construction Survey](https://assets.kpmg.com/content/dam/kpmg/be/pdf/BE-2023-Global-Construction-survey.pdf) describes contractors working on “paper-thin margins that leave little room for error.” In the same survey of 267 owners and contractors, 37% said a capital project had missed budget or schedule by 20% or more in the previous year because of weak risk management, up from 32% in 2021.


The damage usually happens in the gaps between systems. Autodesk and FMI surveyed more than 3,900 construction professionals and


[estimated that bad data](https://www.autodesk.com/blogs/construction/autodesk-fmi-study-global-construction-industry-data-strategies/) (inaccurate, incomplete, inconsistent, or late) cost the global industry $1.85 trillion in 2020, including $88.69 billion of rework.


### **What a small miss does to a thin margin**


Take a $5 million job at that 5.94% net margin: about $297,000 of profit. Assume materials make up 40% of the contract, or $2 million. The Associated General Contractors of America found that


[nonresidential construction input prices rose 7.1%](https://news.agc.org/economics/construction-input-costs-remain-sharply-higher-than-a-year-ago-despite-june-decline-as-aluminum-copper-and-steel-prices-continue-to-climb/) from June 2025 to June 2026, while contractors’ bid prices rose only 3.5%. If your material rates are a year old and you cannot pass the rise on, that 7.1% costs $142,000, nearly half the job’s profit.


Price movement is only one cause; our breakdown of


[why construction projects go over budget](https://rdash.ai/blog/why-do-construction-projects-go-over-budget/) covers the others.


### **The five links of the estimate chain**


Every bid travels through five links. Most estimating software is built for the first three. Profit is protected or lost in the last two.


1. **Quantify:** Measure from drawings (


[takeoff](https://rdash.ai/blog/what-is-a-construction-takeoff-and-how-does-it-work-2/) ) or receive and check a


[bill of quantities](https://rdash.ai/blog/what-is-a-bill-of-quantities-boq-template-included/) .


2. **Price:** Apply material, labor, and equipment rates, then overhead and


[markup](https://rdash.ai/blog/general-contractor-markup-how-to-calculate/) .


3. **Compete:** Collect and


[level subcontractor quotes](https://rdash.ai/blog/construction-bid-leveling-steps-mistakes/) , then issue the proposal.


4. **Commit:** After award, turn line items into purchase orders and subcontracts.


5. **Control:** Track committed, actual, and installed cost against the estimate, plus change orders and billing, through


[job costing](https://rdash.ai/blog/construction-job-costing-a-complete-guide/) .


### **Run the single line item test before you buy anything**


Pick one line from a job you won last year, such as 2,400 sq ft of gypsum partition or 180 m of cable tray. Trace it from drawing to takeoff, priced estimate, subcontractor quote, purchase order, supplier invoice, and cost report. Count every time someone retyped its quantity or rate.


Our rule of thumb: three or more retypes means your problem is handoffs, not takeoff speed. A faster takeoff tool will not fix it. Run the same line through every tool you demo.

## **The 10 Estimating Tools Reviewed and Ranked**


Here are the ten tools in ranked order for general contractors, with what each does well, what it costs, and where it falls short.


### **1. RDash: Best for GCs Who Need the Estimate to Run the Job**


**RDash is not a takeoff tool. It is the system your estimate moves into, built around the bill of quantities, and that is where most GCs win or lose the margin they bid.**


RDash started inside a construction company. Its founders ran


[91Squarefeet](https://rdash.ai/about/) , an in-house design-and-build firm that fitted out offices and retail stores, and the first version of RDash went live on those projects in April 2022. They closed the construction arm in December 2024 to avoid competing with customers.


RDash is backed by


**Y Combinator** ,


**Stellaris Venture Partners** and


**Zacua Ventures** , and co-founder and CEO Amit Bansal presented a


[RICS webinar on BOQ-centric project execution](https://www.rics.org/training-events/online-training/scheduled/south-asia-boq-centric-project-execution-webinar) in February 2026.


**How it handles estimating:** The


[BOQ sits at the center](https://rdash.ai/project-and-design-management/#sec-4-boq-change-orders) of everything. You build it from a master catalog of items (


[element library](https://rdash.ai/power-features/#sec-4-element-libraries) ) or import it from Excel. Each scope item can be broken into materials and assemblies through a


[bill of materials](https://rdash.ai/procurement-and-finance-management/#sec-4-bill-of-materials) , which gives you rate analysis from the material breakdown. Supplier


[rate contracts](https://rdash.ai/procurement-and-finance-management/#sec-1-rate-contracts) link to the same library, so agreed rates pull into vendor orders in one click.


**How it handles the client:** Clients get their own login. They confirm or query individual scope items instead of signing the last page of a 200-line spreadsheet, and every BOQ item keeps its change history. Scope changes run through


[change order](https://rdash.ai/blog/construction-change-orders-explained/) approval workflows, the point where variation disputes tend to start. Our guide to


[creating and sharing a BOQ with clients](https://rdash.ai/blog/how-to-create-and-share-a-boq-with-clients-step-by-step-guide/) walks through it.


**How it carries the estimate after award:** Orders are placed against BOQ items, budget guardrails sit on BOQ elements, and items that start losing margin are flagged at item level. Material receipts, site expenses, supplier running and final bills, and installed progress all tie back to the same line. Standard integrations push POs, invoices, payments, and expenses to Tally, Zoho, Odoo, SAP, Open ERP, Microsoft Business Central, and Oracle.


**Evidence from named projects.** These figures are published on the website and can be verified there.


- **GD Waldner India:** an $8 million MEP package for an energy storage R&D facility in Bengaluru, with 3,600+ line items, 30+ vendors, and $5 million of vendor orders reconciled against $4.4 million of client billing (


[project case study](https://rdash.ai/gd-waldner-project/) ).


- **Occasion Interiors:** a Dubai design-build fit-out firm that moved off a split Excel-and-Zoho estimating stack, has delivered 41 projects on RDash, and traces every request from purchase request to LPO to GRN.


- **Om Sai Intex:** a ₹643 crore interior fit-out contractor that reports 100% of POs traced to the BOQ after a three-to-four-month rollout.


**What is live and what is coming.** Live today: an AI Copilot for prompt-based questions on margins and delays, plus analytics and predictive risk agents. RDash’s Costing Agent, which it says will auto-quantify a BOQ and check historical rates, is still marked “coming soon”. For a feature-by-feature view, see


[RDash vs other construction management software](https://rdash.ai/comprehensive-features-comparison/) .


**Best for:** general contractors, design-build and fit-out firms, and MEP or specialist contractors whose work is priced and billed against a BOQ, especially those running about USD 5 million to 25 million or more in projects a year.


**Pricing:**[Pro](https://rdash.ai/pricing/) costs $1,000 per user per year, paid annually in advance, for firms with up to USD 25 million of annual project volume. Implementation and onboarding are priced separately. Enterprise, above USD 25 million, is quoted on users and volume.


**Watch out for:**


- No drawing takeoff today. If you measure from PDFs, pair RDash with a takeoff tool and import the quantities.


- Seats are priced per user, so decide which site, procurement, and finance roles need logins before you budget.


- Implementation is a separate line item. Get the go-live date in writing; our


[deployment timeline guide](https://rdash.ai/blog/construction-management-software-deployment-timeline-2026/) shows what a realistic rollout looks like.


### **2. STACK: Best for Cloud Takeoff and Estimating in One Tool**


**STACK is the most complete cloud takeoff-and-estimating tool here for GCs who bid from PDFs and want the whole team working in a browser.**


STACK’s Takeoff & Estimate plans come in three tiers. Free gives you one active project a month, up to 300 plan pages and 50 measurements per project, plus seven days of Pro features. Premium adds unlimited projects, AI takeoffs, symbol search, and an overlay to compare drawing versions. Pro adds the estimating layer: worksheet-style estimates built from items and assemblies, a regional BNI cost library, automatic flags for missing materials, native proposals, and a STACK for Excel integration.


After the bid, STACK leans on other systems. Its ERP connectors, a Pro add-on, sync vendor prices, cost codes, purchase orders, and invoices with your accounting software.


**Best for:** commercial GCs and trade contractors estimating from PDFs who want takeoff and pricing in one cloud workspace.


**Pricing:** Free; Premium $299 and Pro $349 per user per month, billed annually. All subscriptions are 12-month terms, and paying upfront saves 20% against monthly payments.


**Watch out for:** Premium is takeoff only, so budget for Pro if you want estimating. Procurement and cost control after award live in your ERP, not in STACK.


### **3. Togal.AI: Best for AI-First Takeoff on Architectural Drawings**


**Togal.AI is the specialist pick when takeoff volume, not pricing, is your bottleneck.**


Togal uses AI to detect, measure, compare, and label spaces and features on architectural drawings. The Growth plan includes unlimited automated takeoffs, chat prompts, and image or symbol searches, and you can invite collaborators outside your company who do not need their own license. Togal is also listed as an integration on Procore’s estimating page, which helps if you price in Procore.


**Best for:** GC estimating teams doing many area and count takeoffs on architectural sets.


**Pricing:** Growth costs $299 per user per month, billed yearly. Teams of four or more move to a custom Business plan with SSO, onboarding, and a classification library template.


**Watch out for:** Togal is a takeoff tool. Rates, sub-leveling, proposals, and procurement happen somewhere else.


### **4. PlanSwift: Best for Estimators Who Want Installed Desktop Software**


**PlanSwift suits estimators who prefer installed software with drag-and-drop assemblies, and it now ships AI tools of its own.**


PlanSwift, a ConstructConnect product since 2018, combines takeoff and estimating in one installed program and reads PDF, JPG, TIFF, and CAD plans. Both of its annual plans include pre-built trade assemblies, priority support, and two hours of one-on-one training.


Essential includes AI Auto Count, Auto Scale, and Auto Bookmark. Core adds Auto Takeoff, which builds a first pass of areas, lengths and counts. You can try either for 14 days without a credit card.


PlanSwift’s own FAQ confirms both plans are annual subscriptions, not the one-time license some older comparison articles still describe.


**Best for:** estimators who work from one machine and want assemblies, plugins, and Excel import.


**Pricing:** Essential $2,000 and Core $3,000 per seat per year, with discounts on additional seats and volume pricing from 10 licenses.


**Watch out for:** weaker fit for teams collaborating across offices and sites in real time, and nothing carries the estimate into purchasing.


### **5. Autodesk ProEst: Best for Mid-Size and Large GCs in the Autodesk Ecosystem**


**ProEst is a mature cloud estimating suite whose real advantage is the route into Autodesk’s construction platform after award.**


ProEst combines cost estimating, 2D takeoff, and bid-day analysis in the cloud. You can import your own cost data or start from the ProEst Costbook, which Autodesk says holds more than 23,000 lines of regional costing data. Detailed estimates convert into project budgets in Forma Build, part of the platform formerly called Autodesk Construction Cloud.


Two things to know before a demo. Autodesk now sells ProEst only inside its Forma for Preconstruction bundle. It also sells Forma Estimate, a separate estimating product, and its own blog says Forma Estimate does not replace ProEst. Ask your rep which one your firm should standardize on.


**Best for:** GCs already using Autodesk Forma for design coordination or project delivery.


**Pricing:** no price on Autodesk’s ProEst page; you contact sales for a bundle quote.


**Watch out for:** two overlapping Autodesk estimating products, and a bundle purchase even if you only want estimating.


### **6. Procore Estimating: Best for GCs Already Standardized on Procore**


**If Procore already runs your projects, its estimating module is the shortest path from bid to budget, because the estimate never leaves the platform.**


Procore Estimating, which still carries Esticom branding as a Procore company, handles takeoff and estimating in one tool. It extracts quantities from 2D drawings and 3D models, uses AI to detect floor plan areas and auto-count repeated symbols, and prices from a customizable database of parts, assemblies, equipment, and services. Procore says estimates move on to bid, contract, and financials without switching applications.


**Best for:** mid-size and large GCs who already use Procore for project management and financials.


**Pricing:** Procore sells annual contracts with unlimited users and data, and quotes each customer individually.


**Watch out for:** you are really buying into the Procore platform. Without it, the post-award advantage disappears.


### **7. Sage Estimating: Best for Commercial GCs on Sage Accounting**


**Sage Estimating is the long-standing choice for commercial GCs who live on bid day and keep their books in Sage.**


Sage Estimating works with RSMeans, other third-party cost databases, or your own. Its BidMatrix tool processes thousands of bid paths, highlights the lowest subcontractor combination, and tracks MBE and WBE participation. Sage AI flags outlier bids and predicts bidder participation from past projects.


Takeoff runs through eTakeoff Dimension, which reads native PDFs. Estimates connect to Sage Intacct Construction, Sage 300 CRE, and Sage 100 Contractor, so data moves into job costing and accounting without re-entry.


**Best for:** commercial GCs with large subcontract packages and an existing Sage accounting stack.


**Pricing:** not published; ask Sage or a Sage reseller for a quote.


**Watch out for:** the full workflow spans several Sage products, so ask how much implementation and training your team will need.


### **8. Buildxact: Best for Residential Builders and Remodelers**


**Buildxact gives residential builders takeoff, estimating, quoting, and job management on one company-wide price with unlimited users.**


Buildxact’s US plans start with Go, a free tier with five credits for AI estimates and proposals. Foundation adds unlimited users, digital takeoffs, the Blu assembly assistant, custom quote letters, e-signatures, dealer integration, and purchase orders. Pro adds Blu’s estimate generator, job management, schedules, and the Onsite mobile app. Master adds Blu’s takeoff assistant and estimate reviewer, user access controls, and priority support.


**Best for:** home builders, remodelers, and small residential GCs moving off spreadsheets.


**Pricing:** Foundation is $199 per month, or 169 per month billed annually (2,030 a year). Pro is $339 and Master is $509 per month on annual billing. Annual plans save 15% and require a 12-month commitment.


**Watch out for:** it is built for residential work, so large commercial bills of quantities and multi-tier subcontract packages may outgrow it.


### **9. Contractor Foreman: Best Budget All-in-One for Small Crews**


**Contractor Foreman packs estimating, bid management, purchase orders, and job costing into one of the cheapest plans on this list, as long as you read the user limits.**


The headline $49 a month on Contractor Foreman’s pricing page is the Basic plan for one user, billed annually at $588. Standard covers 3 users, Plus 8, Pro 15, and Unlimited any number.


Estimates support bulk and line-item markups, takeoffs come with built-in AI, and the bid manager turns a winning sub bid into a purchase order or subcontract. Job costing reports show which items made or lost money, and the QuickBooks Online integration keeps invoices, bills, and payments in step. Every plan starts with a 30-day free trial, and and above add a 100-day money-back guarantee.


**Best for:** small and mid-size GCs who want one affordable system for estimating, scheduling, field logs, and invoicing.


**Pricing:** billed annually, $49 (1 user), $105 (3 users), $166 (8 users), $221 (15 users) or $332 (unlimited users) per month.


**Watch out for:** the entry price covers one person, and complex commercial bids need deeper estimating than an all-in-one tool offers.


### **10. Clear Estimates: Best for Fast, Template-Driven Remodeling Estimates**


**Clear Estimates is the quickest way for a remodeler or small GC to produce a professional estimate without building a cost database first.**


Clear Estimates ships with a 13,000+ line item database, updated quarterly, and 400+ preloaded templates. Every plan includes unlimited AI estimates, built-in e-signature, and payable invoices. Pro adds AI-powered image and plan uploads, Buildertrend and Zapier-based CRM integrations, ATTOM property data, and extra users at $9 a month each.


**Best for:** residential remodelers and small GCs pricing repeatable scopes.


**Pricing:** Standard $79 per month, or $59 billed annually. Pro $119, or $99 billed annually. Franchise from $249, or from $199 billed annually. All plans have a 30-day free trial and no contract.


**Watch out for:** it is template-driven by design, so it is not built for commercial takeoff, sub-leveling, or procurement.


## **BOQ Markets vs Takeoff Markets: How Your Region Changes the Right Tool**


**When tenders are priced from a bill of quantities, the software that prices, approves, and tracks the BOQ becomes most relevant, not the one that measures drawings fastest.**


Most US-written software guides assume one workflow. The GC measures the drawings, builds an estimate, and later breaks it into a


[schedule of values](https://rdash.ai/blog/understanding-schedule-of-values-sov-in-construction/) for billing. Large parts of the world work differently, and the measurement rules show why.


- **UK and RICS markets:** RICS’s


[NRM 2 (2nd edition, October 2021)](https://www.rics.org/content/dam/ricsglobal/documents/standards/october_2021_nrm_2.pdf) sets standard rules for measuring and describing building work in a bill of quantities. It treats the priced BOQ as a contract document that also serves as the basis for valuing work done for interim payments and for budgetary control after award.


- **India:** The Bureau of Indian Standards’


[IS 1200 series](https://law.resource.org/pub/in/bis/S03/is.1200.1.1992.pdf) sets methods of measurement for building and civil works. Its foreword notes that measurement matters from the first estimate through to the final settlement of payments.


### **What changes when the BOQ is the contract**


When the BOQ is the contract, three things matter more than takeoff speed:


1. **Version control:** Every addendum and re-measure creates a new BOQ version, and the team must know which one was priced and which one was approved.


2. **Item-level approval:** Disputes are usually about which line items the client confirmed, not about the total. See our guide to


[BOQ in tendering](https://rdash.ai/blog/boq-in-tendering-the-blueprint-for-winning-bids/) .


3. **Payment against measured items:** Interim bills are valued against the same lines, so the BOQ has to stay connected to installed progress and supplier invoices.


That is why a BOQ-first platform such as RDash does the heavy lifting in these markets, and a takeoff tool becomes the instrument you use to check or re-measure quantities. In hard-bid US work, the order often flips: the takeoff tool leads, and the post-award system receives the result.

**Enterprise GCs:** Integration, permissions, and audit trails outweigh features. The platform you already run for projects and accounting usually decides the estimating tool, so test the integration, not the demo.

### **Who carries the risk when AI gets a quantity wrong**


Duane Morris attorneys Robert Bell and Michael Ferri


[wrote](https://blogs.duanemorris.com/techlaw/2025/09/30/artificial-intelligence-errors-for-construction-contractors/) that early signs point to courts treating AI errors in bids like any other bidding mistake, which leaves the contractor responsible. Put four controls in place before you lean on AI quantities:


1. **Spot-check every submission.** Measure a sample of sheets by hand and compare.


2. **Read the specification, not just the drawings.** AI measures what is drawn; scope hidden in specs and notes still needs a person.


3. **Write down your measurement rules** (NRM 2, IS 1200, or your own house standard), so AI output is checked against something fixed.


4. **Record who reviewed which quantities,** so the sign-off is clear if a claim comes later.

## **Five Mistakes GCs Make When Switching Estimating Software**


**Most failed switches are data and process failures, not software failures.** The estimating errors themselves, from missed scope to stale rates, are covered in our guide to


[construction estimating steps and mistakes](https://rdash.ai/blog/construction-estimating-steps-benefits-and-mistakes/) .


1. **Migrating a stale cost database:** Old rates flow straight into new bids. Input prices rose 7.1% in a year, and about 70% of firms in the AGC and Sage 2026 outlook said tariffs had affected them. Re-price your highest-value items before go-live.


2. **Using different codes for estimating and accounting:** If the estimate and the job cost ledger use different item or cost codes, budget-versus-actual never lines up. Agree on one item library before importing anything; our free


[construction estimate template](https://rdash.ai/blog/construction-estimate-template-free-download/) is a reasonable starting structure.


3. **Buying seats only for estimators:** Retyping happens where the estimate lands: purchasing, project managers, and site engineers. Include them in the trial.


4. **Judging on takeoff speed alone:** A faster takeoff does nothing for the four links after it. Run the single line item test on every shortlisted tool.


5. **Skipping a parallel bid:** Price at least one live tender in the old and new systems side by side, compare line by line, and only then switch the old one off.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **What is the best estimating software for general contractors?**


RDash is the best choice for general contractors whose estimate has to become the working budget, purchase orders, and cost control, because it keeps every BOQ line connected from bid to final bill. For fast takeoff from drawings, STACK and Togal.AI lead. Firms already on Procore, Autodesk, or Sage should start with those vendors’ estimating modules.


### **Is a GRN legally required, or is it just best practice?**


Construction estimating software calculates what a project will cost to build. It measures or imports quantities, applies material, labor, equipment, and subcontract rates, adds overhead and markup, and produces a bid or proposal. Stronger tools also carry the estimate into purchasing, budgets, and job costing after award.


### **What is the difference between takeoff software and estimating software?**


Takeoff software measures quantities from drawings: areas, lengths, and counts. Estimating software turns those quantities into a price by applying material, labor, and equipment rates, overhead, and markup. STACK Pro, PlanSwift, and Procore Estimating do both; Togal.AI focuses on takeoff, and BOQ-centered platforms like RDash carry the priced quantities through purchasing and billing.


### **How much does construction estimating software cost?**


Published plans run from free (STACK Free, Buildxact Go) to $349 per user per month (STACK Pro, billed annually). Company plans such as Contractor Foreman and Buildxact charge a flat monthly price for a set number of users. RDash Pro costs $1,000 per user per year plus implementation. Procore, Sage, and Autodesk ProEst quote privately.


### **Is there free estimating software for general contractors?**


Yes, but with limits. STACK’s free plan allows one active project a month, up to 300 plan pages and 50 measurements per project. Buildxact Go is free with five credits for AI estimates and proposals. Contractor Foreman, Clear Estimates, and PlanSwift offer free trials rather than free plans, and free tiers suit occasional small bids, not a full estimating department.


### **Can AI do construction takeoffs accurately?**


AI is good at repetitive measurement: detecting rooms and areas, counting symbols, and drafting a first-pass takeoff. It does not read scope buried in specifications, and legal commentators expect contractors to stay responsible for AI errors in submitted bids. Treat AI output as a draft that an estimator checks against the drawings, the specification, and your measurement rules.


### **Which estimating software connects to accounting systems like QuickBooks?**


Contractor Foreman integrates with QuickBooks Online. STACK offers ERP connectors as a Pro add-on. Sage Estimating connects to Sage Intacct Construction, Sage 300 CRE, and Sage 100 Contractor, and ProEst feeds budgets into Autodesk Forma Build. RDash syncs POs, invoices, payments, and expenses with Tally, Zoho, Odoo, SAP, Open ERP, Microsoft Business Central, and Oracle.


### **What is a BOQ, and do US general contractors need BOQ software?**


A bill of quantities (BOQ) lists every item of work with a description, unit, and quantity. Once priced, it often becomes a contract document used to value interim payments. US GCs more often work from their own takeoff and a schedule of values, but BOQ-style software still helps any firm that wants each line tracked from estimate to purchase order to invoice.


### **Is cloud or desktop estimating software better?**


Cloud tools such as STACK, Togal.AI and RDash suit teams that share estimates across offices and sites, because everyone works on the same live data. Installed tools such as PlanSwift suit estimators who work from one machine and prefer local files. Most products on this list are cloud-first, so check how any desktop tool shares data with the rest of your team.


### **How long does it take to implement estimating software?**


A takeoff tool can be running within hours; STACK says


[most teams are up and running in a few hours](https://www.stackct.com/pricing/) . A platform that also runs procurement and finance takes longer, and RDash customer Om Sai Intex describes a three-to-four-month rollout. Put the go-live date and the owner on both sides into the contract before you sign.

We could not trace that widely repeated figure to a primary study, so we do not use it. Verifiable data points the same way: in
